INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae  are leading scholars, scientists, and
clinical practitioners in wound ballistics, trauma surgery,
public health, and firearms history and law. 2 Amici
have spent their careers studying the mechanics of
ballistic injury, treating victims of firearm violence, analyzing population-level firearm trauma, and researching
the historical and legal regulation of lethal weaponry.
Amici submit this brief to assist the Court by
providing objective, empirical evidence regarding the
biomechanical and ballistic profile of AR-15-style
semiautomatic rifles—specifically, how high muzzle
velocity, energy transfer, and cavitation produce exceptional tissue lethality compared to standard handguns
and historic long guns. This empirical analysis bears
directly on whether such firearms constitute
“dangerous and unusual” weapons under the Second
Amendment’s historical tradition of arms regulation.

and critical care surgeon at Yale New Haven Hospital’s
Level 1 Trauma Center and an  Associate Professor of
Surgery at Yale School of Medicine.

Epidemiology and Chair of the Department of

Investigator of two CDC-funded research institutions:
the Columbia Center for Injury Science and Prevention

SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Under this Court’s jurisprudence, the Second
Amendment inquiry is “whether the challenged
regulation is consistent with the principles  that
underpin our regulatory tradition.” United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024). The historical
tradition rests on the principle of regulating “dangerous
and unusual weapons” to protect the public from
exceptional threats of harm. District of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 627 (2008). Applying that
principle requires judges to ask a practical question:
What is this weapon capable of doing?
Lethality is an objective measure of dangerousness.
It is a physical property of the weapon, determined by
its design and the laws of physics: the energy its
projectile delivers to the human body, the damage that
energy does to tissue, and the speed, accuracy, and
repetition with which the weapon can deliver every
round. Lethality looks past categorical labels,
appearance, marketing, and resemblance to earlier
firearms. It measures a weapon’s capacity to harm.
To assist the Court’s analysis, Amici present newly
available empirical evidence that demonstrates the
lethal capacity of various modern and historical
firearms across the same objective metrics. Those
measurements provide a common basis for evaluating

5

the inherent lethality of the AR-15 3 against modern
and historical firearms.
The physics is undeniable. Across every objective
lethality metric, the AR-15 is nothing like the
handguns addressed in Heller. By contrast, across
those same metrics, the AR-15 is functionally
indistinguishable from the U.S. military’s M16. This
makes sense: the AR-15 was specifically designed to
empower U.S. soldiers to  exert extraordinary lethal
force on the battlefield.
And the AR-15’s phenomenal lethality is not
confined to a single shot. It s destructive force can be
delivered rapidly, accurately, and repeatedly. The
result is extraordinary ev en by modern standards:
lethal force that once required a battalion of armed
individuals is now concentrated in a single weapon
and a single shooter. A lone individual armed with an
AR-15 can murder classrooms full of children,
religious worshippers, concertgoers, families at a
Fourth of July parade, and ordinary people doing their
grocery shopping in minutes.
Amici urge the Court to evaluate these weapons for
what they are: what they were designed for, how they
are used, and what they do . By that measure, AR-15s
and similar semiautomatic rifles are extraordinarily
lethal. Governments in the United States have long
regulated and even banned weapons like them. The
Court should look past sales figures, the label “rifle,”
and superficial mechanical similarities between the
challenged firearms and other firearms. Banning the
AR-15 does not violate the Second Amendment.

ARGUMENT
I. THE SECOND AMENDMENT INQUIRY
HAS ALWAYS BEEN CONCERNED WITH
DANGEROUSNESS
This case asks whether the Second Amendment permits
state and local governments to enact regulations
prohibiting certain AR-15 platform rifles. Under the
test announced in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n
v. Bruen, courts must determine whether a challenged
regulation is “consistent with this Nation’s historical
tradition of firearm regulation,” recognizing that
“cases implicating unprecedented societal concerns or
dramatic technological changes may require a more
nuanced approach” to that historical inquiry. 597 U.S.
1, 17, 27 (2022). Rahimi makes clear that historical
“precedents were not meant to suggest a law trapped
in amber.” 602 U.S. at 691. The relevant inquiry is
“whether the challenged regulation is consistent with
the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.”
Id. at 692 (emphasis added).
Those principles consistently converge on a core
concept: dangerousness. In District of Columbia v.
Heller, the Court recognized this Nation’s historical
tradition of regulating “dangerous and unusual” weapons.
554 U.S. at 627. The Founding generation would have
understood that phrase as  a hendiadys: two words
joined to express a single idea, much like “cruel and
unusual” or “nice and hot.” See Darrell A.H. Miller et
al., Lethality and the Historical Principles of Arms
Regulation, 54 Pepperdine L. Rev. (forthcoming 2026)
(manuscript at 3).4 It thus describes weapons that are
unusually dangerous or exceptionally dangerous. See
Samuel L. Bray, “Necessary and Proper” and “Cruel

4 https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7525418

7

and Unusual”: Hendiadys in the Constitution, 102 Va.
L. Rev. 687, 699 (2016). Blackstone points the same
way, describing the long-accepted offense at common
law of “riding or going armed, with dangerous or
unusual weapons, [to] terrify[] the good people of the
land.” 4 William Blackstone, Commentaries on the
Laws of England 148–149 (1769); see Rahimi, 602 U.S.
at 697. As the Seventh Circuit recently explained,
“[u]sing one or another label—‘dangerous and unusual,’
‘unusually dangerous,’ ‘especially dangerous,’ ‘particularly
capable of unprecedented lethality’”—nearly every
court to confront the issue has “coalesced around a
largely overlapping set of historical regulations imposing
targeted restrictions on weapons whose danger and
lethality stand out.” Barnett v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035,
1047 (7th Cir. 2026) (St. Eve, J.). See, e.g., Ocean State
Tactical, LLC v. Rhode Island , 95 F.th 38,44–52 (1st
Cir. 2024); Capen v. Campbell, 134 F.4th 660, 669–73
(1st Cir. 2025); Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rts. v. Lamont, 153
F.4th 213, 240–47 (2d Cir. 2025); Bianchi v. Brown, 111
F.4th 438, 464–72 (4th Cir. 2024); Duncan v. Bonta, 133
F.4th 852, 874–84 (9th Cir. 2026); Hanson v. District of
Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 234–40 (D.C. Cir. 2024).
The historical tradition responded to exceptional
dangers a weapon posed to public safety. See Miller et
al., Lethality, supra, at 32–43. Dangerousness is not to
be considered in the abstract.  It asks what a weapon
enables its user to do and the danger that capability
poses to human life and public safety. The
constitutional significance of a weapon lies not in what
it is called, what it looks like, or how popular it is, but
in what it is capable of doing. See id. at 32–33.
Lethality is the most direct and objective measure of
dangerousness. Id. at 20–23. It is an inherent function
of the weapon’s technological design and the laws of

8

physics. A firearm’s capacity to kill and injure derives
from physical characteristics that can be observed and
compared: the velocity with which it fires a projectile,
the energy with which that projectile impacts the
human body, the resulting tissue damage, and the
speed, accuracy, and repetition with which that force
can be delivered. Those metrics permit courts to
compare weapons across different designs, technologies,
and historical eras using common objective criteria. Id.
at 26–28.
Lethality looks beyond appearance and superficial
resemblance to historical predecessors. It cuts through
marketing and categorical labels. And it is indifferent
to popularity and manufacturing statistics. Instead, it
asks a concrete question: how dangerous is the weapon,
measured by what it is inherently capable of doing?
II. AR-15 PLATFORM RIFLES ARE
EXTRAORDINARILY LETHAL IN
ABSOLUTE AND COMPARATIVE TERMS
Objective measurements of lethality become
especially clear through comparison. Heller supplies
two natural benchmarks: the handgun, which the
Court identified as the “quintessential self-defense
weapon,” and the M16, which is among the weapons
that the Court described as “most useful in military
service” and that “may be banned.” 554 U.S. at 627, 629.
Much of the evidence regarding the AR-15’s lethality
comes from clinical, forensic, and other first-hand
observations of the injuries it causes. The evidence is
powerful and directly related to the “unprecedented
societal concerns” that have motivated efforts to
regulate these dangerous weapons. Bruen, 597 U.S. at
27. Because photographs of the horrific wounds caused
by an AR-15 are too shocking to be released for public

9

review, critics have debated the veracity or weight of
these observations, arguing that the descriptions are
“overdramatized” or “exaggerated” and reflect factors
other than the firearm itself. Brief of Amici Curiae
Ballistics Experts & Second Amend. Law Professors in
Supp. of Pet’rs (“Ballistics Amicus Br.”) 25–27.
Newly available empirical data settles that debate
by providing objective evidence of the AR-15’s lethality
compared to modern and historical firearms.
A. New Empirical Data Permit Direct,
Objective Comparison of the AR-15’s
Lethality
Recent advances in synthetic ballistic gelatin and
high-speed video technology made it possible for
researchers to test a wide range of firearms under
uniform conditions and measure tissue damage
metrics—such as velocity, energy transfer, and
temporary cavity formation—with a level of precision
that earlier studies could not achieve.
The first-of-its-kind peer-reviewed comparative
study published in Forensic Science, Medicine and
Pathology provides objective evidence of a weapon’s
capacity for injury. See Joseph LeSueur et al.,
Experimental Wound Ballistic Study to Understand
Biomechanical Differences in Gunshot Wounds from
Various Bullets and Firearms, 22 Forensic Sci., Med. &
Pathology 277 (2026). 5 An interdisciplinary team from
the Medical College of Wisconsin and Marquette
University’s Departments of  Biomedical Engineering,
Neurosurgery , Surgery and Emergency Medicine, and
the Comprehensive Injury Center, working with the
Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Firearms and

5 https://perma.cc/V69S-B7K6

10

Toolmark Analysis Unit, tested 21 firearm-andammunition combinations, including handguns, a
nineteenth-century lever-action rifle, an AR-15, an
M16, and a submachine gun. Id. at 279. Each weapon
was fired into synthetic ballistic gelatin blocks
approximating the tissue depth of an adult human
torso or limb. Id. The gelatin was validated against
human and animal data to accurately simulate
biological muscle tissue. Id. at 278. Pressure sensors
and high-speed video (capturing up to 100,000 frames
per second) were used to quantify a bullet’s effects at
the moments of and immediately after impact. Id. at
281. Because every round was tested in the same
validated medium under identical conditions, the
study was able to isolate differences attributable to the
firearms themselves. Id. at 279, 284.
The table below shows th e measurements collected
for firearms relevant to this Court’s Second Amendment
jurisprudence: a Founding-era musket; a Winchester
1873 rifle; modern handguns; the AR-15, and the M16.6

Physics explains the AR-15’s extraordinary lethality.
Kinetic energy is measured as one-half of the bullet
mass multiplied by the square of the bullet’s velocity
[½ (Bullet Mass) × (Velocity) 2]. LeSueur et al., supra,
at 280. Thus, speed of the projectile is the critical
engine of destructive force.
An AR-15 fires a light, thin bullet at extraordinary
speed: more than 3,200 feet per second. That is more
than twice the speed of sound, and more than twice the
velocity of the fastest handgun round (the 9mm) fired.
The resulting energy transferred from the projectile
into its target—a direct indicator of the damage the
projectile will cause—was more than ten times greater
for the AR-15 (1612 joules) than for the 9mm handgun
(155 joules).

supra, at 279, 281. Velocity and cavity diameter measurements
were converted from metric to imperial units.

12

As a projectile penetrates the surface of its target, it
sets surrounding material in motion, driving it
outward around the channel through which the bullet
passes. Id. at 278.  The resulting expansion is the socalled “temporary cavity,” which reflects how
extensively, and where, the surrounding material was
displaced. Id. In the human body, that material is
comprised of tissue, organs, blood vessels, nerves, and
sometimes bone. The violent displacement in biological
tissue caused by the temporary cavity results in

states, including restrictions designed to prevent their
acquisition and possession. See, e.g., 1837 Ala. Acts 7;
1838 Tenn. Pub. Acts 200; 1881 Ark. Acts 191, 192. The
historical tradition did not treat common use and
dangerousness as mutually exclusive concepts. To the
contrary, widespread possession often brought a
weapon’s dangers into sharper focus, and thus
impelled governments to re spond. History does not
support a rule where mass distribution becomes a
constitutional safe harbor for exceptionally dangerous
weapons.
Nor was the Bowie knife immunized because it
belonged to the broader category of “knives.”
Governments regulated that unusually dangerous
type of knife, while leaving the public free to buy steak
knives and other knives for self-defense. So too here:

30

An AR-15 is a semiautomatic rifle, but calling it a
“rifle” does not immunize this exceptionally lethal type
of rifle from regulation any more than calling a Bowie
knife a “knife” did historically. The challenged laws do
not constitute a categorical ban on rifles; they prohibit
a particular subset of rifles that pose an exceptional
danger to the public. The Second Amendment inquiry
does not turn on finding the lowest common
denominator into which a weapon can be classified. It
asks whether the regulation  is consistent with the
principles reflected in our historical tradition. Rahimi,
602 U.S. at 692.
The point is not that Bowie knives were as lethal as
modern firearms, much less AR-15s. But governments
have always had the power to regulate, and even
prohibit, implements of exceptional lethality. Miller et
al., Lethality, supra, at 41–42. The historical principle
is sound, and modern medical science allows that
principle to be applied with greater precision. Rather
than relying on categorical labels, manufacturing
statistics, or assumptions, courts can examine what a
weapon actually does and compare its capacity for
harm with that of other weapons. The data presented
here provide a better-informed basis for identifying
weapons that are exceptionally dangerous. Here, the
evidence is clear. The AR-15’s unprecedented capacity
for lethality is not conjecture, stereotype, or label. It is
a measurable and undeniable fact.
CONCLUSION
For centuries, American legislatures have responded
to weapons of exceptional danger with regulation. The
principle has never changed: the Second Amendment
protects the arms of ordinary self-defense, but it does
not disable government from confronting weapons
whose destructive power sets them apart. The

31

enduring principle of dangerousness does not ask the
Court to suspend reality.
The reality here is explained by physics. The AR-15
was designed to deliver extraordinary force. It does so
with devastating effect. Its bullets strike with several
times the energy of a hand gun round, create wound
cavities of an entirely different magnitude, destroy
tissue far beyond the bullet's path, and inflict injuries
that highly trained medical professionals cannot
repair. Measured by every objective metric, it is
materially indistinguishable from the U.S. military’s
M16 when fired semiautomatically.
The Constitution has always preserved the right of
self-defense while permitting governments to regulate
weapons of extraordinary danger to protect their
communities.
Amici respectfully submit that the judgments of the
Seventh and Second Circuits be affirmed.
